cards.front: What is the center of mass of a system?
cards.back: The **mass-weighted average position** of all the parts of the system. A system's mass can be treated as if it were concentrated at this point when describing its overall motion.

cards.front: Which forces change the overall motion of a system?
cards.back: Only the **net external force**. Internal forces come in equal and opposite pairs, so they cancel when you add the forces on the whole system.
cards.hint: Think about where each force comes from relative to your chosen system.

cards.front: How does the center of mass of a system accelerate?
cards.back: $a_{\mathrm{cm}}=\frac{F_{\mathrm{net,ext}}}{M}$, where $M$ is the **total mass** of the system and $F_{\mathrm{net,ext}}$ is the net external force. Internal forces play no part.
cards.hint: Only forces from outside the system appear in the numerator.

cards.front: What is a system in physics?
cards.back: The **object or group of objects** you choose to analyze. Everything else is the surroundings.
A **force between parts of the same system**. Internal forces cancel when you add the forces on the whole system.

cards.front: What is an external force on a system?
cards.back: A **force exerted on the system by an object outside it**, such as gravity from Earth. The net external force sets how the center of mass accelerates.
cards.hint: Ask whether the object pushing or pulling is inside your chosen system.

cards.front: Where is the center of mass of a uniform, symmetric object such as a ring?
cards.back: At its **geometric center**, found by symmetry. For a uniform ring this point lies in the empty middle, outside the material.
cards.hint: Locate it by symmetry before doing any calculation.

cards.front: What is the formula for the center of mass of separate masses on a line?
cards.back: $x_{\mathrm{cm}}=\frac{m_1x_1+m_2x_2+\cdots}{m_1+m_2+\cdots}$, a **weighted average** where each position is weighted by its mass. Heavier masses pull the center toward themselves.
cards.hint: Choose an origin first and measure every position from it.

cards.front: What steps find the center of mass of two masses on a line?
cards.back: 1) Choose an origin. 2) Write $x_{\mathrm{cm}}=\frac{m_1x_1+m_2x_2}{m_1+m_2}$. 3) Substitute the masses and positions. 4) Work out the numerator and denominator, then divide.
cards.hint: Check the answer lies between the masses and closer to the heavier one.

cards.front: Where is the center of mass of a 2.0 kg cart at $x=0$ and a 6.0 kg cart at $x=4.0\ \mathrm{m}$?
cards.back: $x_{\mathrm{cm}}=3.0\ \mathrm{m}$. The working is $\frac{(2.0)(0)+(6.0)(4.0)}{2.0+6.0}=\frac{24}{8.0}$, which sits closer to the heavier cart.

cards.front: Your center of mass for two masses on a line comes out outside the range between them. What went wrong?
cards.back: An **arithmetic slip**. For two masses on a line, the center of mass must lie between them and closer to the larger mass.

cards.front: A student says moving parts mean the center of mass must move. Is this right?
cards.back: No. Parts can move in opposite directions while the **center of mass stays put**. It moves only when a net external force acts.

cards.front: Two skaters start at rest on frictionless ice and push apart. What happens to their center of mass?
cards.back: It stays at **rest**. Their pushes are internal forces, and no net external horizontal force acts on the pair, so the center of mass cannot accelerate.

cards.front: What happens to the center of mass if the net external force on a system is zero?
cards.back: It keeps a **constant velocity**, so it does not accelerate. Internal forces play no part in this.
